payload.name: log-frequency-spectrogram
payload.scope: A human-made time-frequency representation that maps a signal's frequency axis to a logarithmic (or other perceptual) scale so that bins are spaced proportionally to their center frequency. It persists through audio analysis libraries and research implementations that compute the representation from a signal's short-time Fourier transform with frequency-axis resampling.

definition.body: A log-frequency spectrogram is a human-made time-frequency representation that maps a signal's spectrum onto a frequency axis whose spacing is proportional to the logarithm of frequency. Its parameters are: (1) the frequency mapping function (logarithmic with a specified base, Mel scale, or equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth scale), (2) the number of frequency bins per octave or decade, (3) the reference frequency and lowest frequency, and (4) the windowing function and hop size used in the underlying short-time Fourier transform. It persists as a computed array in audio analysis libraries (librosa, Essentia, MIRtoolbox) and research code that transforms linear-frequency spectrograms via frequency-axis interpolation. e.g.: librosa.logspec function output; Essentia LogFrequencySpectrum algorithm output; MIRtoolbox logspec function; constant-Q transform spectrogram display | not: constant-q-transform (the algorithm that computes it); linear-frequency spectrogram (frequency axis spaced uniformly in Hz) [formal: specrogramm frequency logarithmica | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: constant-q-transform-derived
payload.scope: A human-made class of time-frequency representations that inherit the constant-Q property from the constant-Q transform — frequency bin bandwidth proportional to center frequency — while differing from the canonical CQT in discretization, window shape, or computational structure. Built for practical audio analysis where the ideal CQT's continuous formulation must be adapted for digital implementation.

definition.body: A constant-Q transform-derived representation is a human-made time-frequency representation that maintains the constant-Q property (bin bandwidth proportional to center frequency) while differing from the canonical constant-Q transform in at least one of: discretization scheme, analysis window shape, or computational structure. Its parameters are: (1) the discretization method (oversampled DFT on geometric frequency grid, filter bank implementation, or zero-padded FFT), (2) the analysis window (Gaussian, Kaiser-Bessel derived, or other constant-Q-preserving window), (3) the quality factor Q and its constancy across frequency, and (4) the overlap and phase treatment. It persists as implementations in audio analysis libraries and research code where the idealized continuous CQT must be adapted for discrete computation. e.g.: librosa.cqt implementation; Essentia ConstantQBands algorithm; Scikit-learn's constant-Q feature extraction; OpenL3 audio embeddings use CQT-derived representation | not: constant-q-transform (the idealized continuous formulation); log-frequency-spectrogram (broader class including non-constant-Q log scaling) [formal: transformatio constantis-Q derivata | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: linear-prediction-coefficient
payload.scope: A human-made set of scalar coefficients that parameterize a linear prediction model for a signal, quantifying how each sample can be estimated as a weighted sum of previous samples. These coefficients form the core representation in speech coding, speaker identification, and spectral analysis.

definition.body: A linear prediction coefficient is a human-made scalar parameter a_k that appears in a linear prediction model where a signal sample x[n] is estimated as a weighted sum of P previous samples: x_hat[n] = sum_{k=1}^{P} a_k x[n-k]. Its parameters are: (1) the prediction order P, determining the number of coefficients, (2) the coefficient values themselves a_1 through a_P, computed via autocorrelation, covariance, or lattice methods, and (3) the normalization convention (whether a_0 = 1 or the coefficients are normalized). It persists through speech coding standards (G.729, ACELP codecs), LPC analysis software (MATLAB lpc, librosa.lpc), and academic implementations across signal processing. e.g.: MATLAB lpc() function output; G.729 CELP codec LSP parameters derived from LPC coefficients; librosa.lpc function output; ITU-T G.721 ADPCM quantizer uses related coefficients | not: linear-prediction-filter (the filter whose transfer function is the reciprocal of the prediction polynomial); reflection-coefficient (parcor coefficients, which are a nonlinear reparameterization of LPC coefficients) [formal: coefficient praedictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: line-spectral-pair
payload.scope: A human-made pair of spectral representations derived from linear prediction coefficients that provide a robust parameterization for speech coding, mapping the LPC polynomial roots to frequencies and line spectral frequencies for stable quantization.

definition.body: A line spectral pair is a human-made pair of spectral representations (line spectral frequencies and line spectral amplitudes) derived from the roots of the LPC prediction polynomial's even and odd parts. Its parameters are: (1) the number of LSP frequencies (typically equal to the LPC prediction order P), (2) their values in radians or normalized frequency, ordered increasingly between 0 and pi, and (3) the quantization scheme used for transmission. It persists through speech coding standards (G.729, AMR, GSM-EFR) that use LSPs instead of raw LPC coefficients for stable interpolation and quantization. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 LSP parameter encoding; AMR codec LSP-to-LPC conversion; GSM-EFR LSP vector quantization; ACELP codebook search uses LSP interpolation | not: linear-prediction-coefficient (raw LPC coefficients, unstable for quantization); line-spectral-frequencies (LSF only, not the full pair including amplitudes) [formal: pares lineares spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: linear-prediction-filter
payload.scope: A human-made all-pole digital filter whose transfer function is the reciprocal of a linear prediction error polynomial, used to synthesize speech or model resonant structures from linear prediction coefficients. It represents the vocal tract or other resonant systems in speech coding.

definition.body: A linear prediction filter is a human-made all-pole digital filter with transfer function H(z) = G / A(z) where G is a gain factor and A(z) = 1 + sum_{k=1}^{P} a_k z^(-k) is the prediction error polynomial. Its parameters are: (1) the prediction coefficients a_k (LPC coefficients), (2) the gain G (scale factor for input excitation), (3) the prediction order P (equal to the number of poles), and (4) the input excitation signal (pulse train for voiced, white noise for unvoiced). It persists as the synthesis filter in speech coding standards (G.729 CELP, AMR), LPC vocoders (AMDF vocoder, Klatt synthesizer), and speech analysis software. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 CELP synthesis filter; Klatt synthesizer all-pole vocoder; MATLAB lfilter with LPC coefficients; librosa lpc synthesis in speech processing | not: prediction-error-filter (the FIR analysis filter with transfer function A(z), not G/A(z)); linear-prediction-coefficient (the scalar parameters a_k, not the filter itself) [formal: filter praedictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

Its parameters are: (1) the prediction coefficients a_k (LPC coefficients), (2) the gain G (scale factor for input excitation), (3) the prediction order P (equal to the number of poles), and (4) the input excitation signal (pulse train for voiced, white noise for unvoiced). It persists as the synthesis filter in speech coding standards (G.729 CELP, AMR), LPC vocoders (AMDF vocoder, Klatt synthesizer), and speech analysis software. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 CELP synthesis filter; Klatt synthesizer all-pole vocoder; MATLAB lfilter with LPC coefficients; librosa lpc synthesis in speech processing | not: prediction-error-filter (the FIR analysis filter with transfer function A(z), not G/A(z)); linear-prediction-coefficient (the scalar parameters a_k, not the filter itself) [formal: filter praedictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

definition.body: An algebraic code-excited linear prediction (ACELP) codec is a human-made speech coding algorithm that represents the residual excitation signal as a sparse linear combination of codewords from an algebraic codebook, filtered through a linear prediction synthesis filter. Its parameters are: (1) the algebraic codebook structure (fixed codebook with sparse impulse positions, e.g., 4 pulses per subframe), (2) the pitch delay (fixed or adaptive codebook), (3) the gain factors for both codebook and pitch excitation, and (4) the linear prediction analysis order and frame length (typically 20ms frames, 160 samples at 8kHz). It persists in ITU-T G.729, ETSI GSM-EFR, and 3GPP AMR speech codecs, implemented in mobile baseband processors and VoIP software. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 Annex B ACELP codec; ETSI GSM-EFR 13 kbps ACELP; 3GPP AMR narrowband mode; Adobe Flash SoundCodec 3 (Speex) uses ACELP variant | not: speech-codec (broader class including MP3, AAC, OPUS); linear-prediction-filter (the synthesis filter component, not the full ACELP algorithm) [formal: codex excitationis algebraicae praedictionis linearis | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: tempogram
payload.scope: A human-made visual representation that maps tempo periodicity over time by computing onset autocorrelation across a range of lag values

definition.body: Tempogram analysis is a music information retrieval technique that reveals tempo periodicity by computing the self-similarity of an onset envelope over varying lag values. The method operates by: (1) computing an onset detection function from the audio signal, (2) computing onset autocorrelation or inter-onset-interval similarity over a range of lag values, and (3) displaying the result as a two-dimensional map where one axis represents lag (or tempo) and the other represents time. Persistence mechanism: implemented in MIR toolkits including librosa and Essentia rhythm analysis modules; taught as a standard visualization technique in rhythm analysis. e.g.: librosa.feature.tempogram; Essentia tempogram extractor; McVicar drum tempogram; Ellis DCJ beat tempogram | not: spectrogram; mel-spectrogram; beat-tracking [formal: tempus-index | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: beat-detection
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing method that classifies individual audio frames as beat or non-beat positions using local onset energy features

definition.body: Beat detection is a real-time audio analysis technique that classifies each frame of a signal as either a beat position or a non-beat position. The method operates by: (1) computing a short-time energy or spectral flux onset function, (2) applying a running-average threshold or adaptive detector to each frame independently, and (3) outputting a binary classification for every frame. Unlike global beat tracking, it produces no tempo estimate or phase alignment — only a frame-level beat/non-beat decision. Persistence mechanism: implemented as standalone algorithms in DJ software, music analysis libraries, and embedded audio processing systems; taught as a fundamental technique in digital signal processing. e.g.: Kubilius onset detector; McVicar drum detection threshold; Essentia BeatDetector; Tzanetakis beat detector | not: beat-tracking; onset-detection; tempo-estimation [formal: pulsus-detectio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spectral-histogram
payload.scope: A human-made audio analysis construct: a set of statistical measures computed over the distribution of spectral energy across frequency bins within an analysis window. It characterizes the shape of the power spectrum using moments — specifically the zeroth moment (total energy), first moment (spectral centroid), skewness (asymmetry of the energy distribution), kurtosis (tailedness of the energy distribution), and flux (rate of change) — providing a compact fixed-size description of spectral shape used in music information retrieval, audio classification, and timbre analysis.

definition.body: Spectral-histogram is a fixed-length feature vector of five statistical moments computed over the power spectrum within each analysis frame. Parameters: (1) the power spectral density estimate at each frequency bin, (2) the frequency center of each bin. The five moments are: zeroth moment (spectral energy — sum of spectral power), first moment (spectral centroid — energy-weighted mean frequency), skewness (normalized third central moment measuring asymmetry of the spectral energy distribution), kurtosis (normalized fourth central moment measuring tailedness of the spectral energy distribution), and spectral flux (sum of squared differences between consecutive frames' spectral energies). The construct persists as a standard feature in MIR toolkits (librosa, Essentia, OpenSMILE), audio classification pipelines, and music information retrieval systems where compact spectral shape description is needed. e.g.: spectral histogram features in the GTZAN genre classification dataset; spectral histogram feature extraction in librosa.feature.spectral_centroid plus librosa.feature.spectral_rolloff; spectral shape features used in the RAVDESS emotional speech database classification pipeline | not: spectral-feature (the broader class of per-bin or per-frame spectral measures); spectral-moment (the general mathematical framework without the fixed five-element histogram composition) [formal: histogramma spectrumle | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spectral-difference-vector
payload.scope: A human-made audio analysis construct: a vector of per-bin absolute differences between consecutive power spectra that quantifies spectral change between adjacent time frames. It provides a frame-by-frame measure of how the spectral content is evolving, serving as a temporal dynamics feature in speech recognition, music transcription, and audio event detection systems.

definition.body: Spectral-difference-vector is a per-frequency-bin measure of absolute change in spectral energy between consecutive analysis frames, computed as the element-wise absolute difference of power spectra. Parameters: (1) the power spectrum at time frame t, (2) the power spectrum at time frame t-1, (3) the frequency bin index f. The construction computes D(f) = |P(f,t) - P(f,t-1)| for each bin, yielding a vector whose magnitude indicates the amount of spectral change and whose bin-wise pattern indicates which frequency regions are changing. The construct persists as a standard feature in audio analysis (librosa.feature.spectral_difference), speech processing (Kaldi spectral-difference computation), and music information retrieval for beat tracking and onset detection. e.g.: spectral_difference feature extraction in librosa.audio feature pipeline; spectral difference-based onset detection in Essentia audio analysis framework; spectral difference features for audio event detection in the AudioSet classification dataset | not: spectral-difference; onset-detection [formal: vector differentiae spectrumli | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: diffusion-model
payload.scope: A human-made generative modeling construct: a class of probabilistic models that learn to generate data by reversing a learned denoising process. The model is trained to progressively remove noise from a corrupted input, starting from pure Gaussian noise and iteratively producing a coherent data sample through a sequence of learned denoising steps parameterized by a neural network.

definition.body: Diffusion-model is a generative probabilistic model that synthesizes data through iterative denoising of a learned reverse diffusion process. Parameters: (1) a forward diffusion process that progressively adds Gaussian noise to training data over T timesteps, (2) a neural network (typically a U-Net architecture) trained to predict and reverse the forward noise addition, (3) the number of timesteps T controlling the granularity of the denoising trajectory. The construction trains by minimizing the variational lower bound on the data likelihood, with the network predicting the noise added at each timestep. Persistence: implemented in major generative AI frameworks (diffusers, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2, Imagen), standardized through the DDPM/DDIM formalisms, and deployed in text-to-image, audio generation, and video synthesis systems. e.g.: Stable Diffusion v2.1 for text-to-image generation; DALL-E 2 for image synthesis from natural language; Imagen for high-resolution text-to-image synthesis; OpenAI's audio diffusion models for text-to-speech | not: variational-autoencoder (latent-space generative model using reparameterization trick, not iterative denoising); flow-matching (deterministic continuous transformation, not stochastic denoising process) [formal: model diffusio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: score-matching
payload.scope: A human-made generative modeling construct: a class of probabilistic training methods that learn to score data by estimating the gradient of the log probability density function (the score) at each point in the data space. These methods enable likelihood-free training of generative models by matching the model's predicted score to the true data score, without requiring explicit likelihood evaluation.

definition.body: Score-matching is a probabilistic training method that learns generative models by matching the model's predicted score (gradient of the log density) to the true data score, enabling likelihood-free training. Parameters: (1) a parametric score function (neural network) sθ(x) approximating ∇x log p_data(x), (2) a noise-level parameterization for multi-scale score estimation, (3) the matching objective — typically the Fisher divergence or denoising score matching loss. The construction estimates the score function by minimizing the difference between the model's predicted score and the score of the noised data distribution. Persistence: formalized in Song & Ermon 2019 denoising score matching framework, implemented in score-based generative modeling libraries, foundational to score SDE frameworks used in modern diffusion models. e.g.: Song & Ermon 2019 denoising score matching for continuous normalizing flows; Song et al. 2021 score-based generative modeling through SDEs; Dhariwal & Nichol 2021 diffusion models using score-matching objectives | not: maximum-likelihood-estimation (which requires explicit likelihood computation); variational-inference (which approximates the posterior distribution, not the data score) [formal: aequatio graduum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: hidden-markov-model
payload.scope: Made so that a hidden state sequence can be inferred and its likelihood evaluated from an observation sequence, when the states themselves are not directly observable — the case of classical speech recognition and sequence analysis.

definition.body: A hidden Markov model (HMM) is a human-made probabilistic model of a process whose state evolves as a Markov chain but is not directly observed: a finite state set, a state-to-state transition matrix A, an emission model B for the observation at each state, and an initial-state distribution pi. From these parameters the model computes the three canonical inferences: the likelihood of an observation sequence (forward algorithm), the single most likely hidden state sequence (Viterbi algorithm), and the smoothed state posteriors (forward-backward), with the parameters themselves learned from data by the Baum-Welch (expectation-maximization) procedure. Parameters: (1) number of states N, (2) the observation alphabet — discrete symbols or a continuous emission density, typically Gaussian mixtures, (3) the transition matrix A, (4) the emission model B, (5) the initial distribution pi. Persistence: taught as the canonical probabilistic model in speech, signal processing and sequence-analysis curricula, implemented in standard toolkits (HTK, Kaldi, the Baum-Welch references), and used as the acoustic backbone of classical large-vocabulary speech recognition. e.g.: the 39-state triphone HMM of HTK's classical large-vocabulary speech recognizer; the four-state HMM for exon/intron segmentation in the Durbin et al. Bioinformatics textbook; the Baum-Welch-trained HMM for vowel segmentation of TIMIT speech; the two-state HMM for tracking an unobserved regime in a financial time series | not: a Markov chain (all states observed, no emissions); a finite-state automaton (deterministic transitions, no probabilities); a dynamic Bayesian network (arbitrary directed topology, not a linear state sequence) [formal: machina markovi occulta | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: markov-chain
payload.scope: Made to model a sequence whose next step depends only on the current step, so that the future is conditionally independent of the past given the present state.

definition.body: A Markov chain is a human-made stochastic process whose next state depends only on the current state, not on the path that reached it: a state space S, a transition structure P giving the law of the next state given the current one, and an initial distribution. The defining property — P(X_{n+1} | X_1..X_n) = P(X_{n+1} | X_n) — is the Markov property. From it the process yields the joint distribution of any trajectory, the stationary (equilibrium) distribution, and hitting-time behavior. Parameters: (1) the state space (finite, countable, or continuous), (2) the transition matrix or kernel P, (3) the initial distribution, (4) the time index (discrete or continuous). Persistence: taught as the canonical dependent-sequence model in probability, statistics and stochastic processes; the backbone of Monte Carlo Markov chain simulation (Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs), of PageRank's random-surfer model, and of the original 1906 letter-sequence study of Pushkin's Eneida that introduced it. e.g.: the transition matrix of Page and Brin's random-surfer web model that underlies PageRank; the Metropolis-Hastings MCMC sampler whose proposals form a Markov chain over parameter space; the two-state birth-death chain modeling an open population with immigration and death; Markov's 1906 chain for the vowel-to-consonant transitions in Pushkin's Eneida | not: an i.i.d. sequence (no dependence on the current state); a Poisson process (continuous-time, independent increments, no state-dependent transition) [formal: catena markovi | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: levinson-durbin
payload.scope: People made the Levinson-Durbin algorithm to recursively solve the Yule-Walker equations for autoregressive parameter estimation without computing the full matrix inverse.

definition.body: The Levinson-Durbin algorithm is a human-made recursive method for solving the system of linear equations that arises in autocorrelation-based linear prediction analysis. It computes reflection coefficients and prediction filter coefficients at each order m=1..p using the previous order solution, avoiding the O(p^3) matrix inversion of direct methods. The recurrence: at each step, the reflection coefficient k_m is computed from forward and backward prediction errors, and the order-m prediction coefficients are updated from the order-(m-1) coefficients using k_m. The algorithm also computes the prediction error power at each order. It guarantees the absolute value of each reflection coefficient is less than 1, ensuring stability. Parameters: the autocorrelation sequence r(0) through r(p), the prediction order p. Persistence: implemented in all standard linear prediction toolboxes and taught as the canonical solver for Toeplitz systems. e.g.: the Levinson-Durbin recursion in R. E. Kalman 1960 work on linear prediction; the algorithm as implemented in MATLAB lpc function; the Durbin recursion for AR model fitting in the R forecast package | not: Levinson recursion (applies to Toeplitz systems more broadly, not restricted to autocorrelation); Cholesky decomposition (direct factorization without recursion) [formal: recursio levinson | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: score-sampling
payload.scope: People made score-based sampling to draw data samples from complex probability distributions by following the gradient of the log-density (score) without needing the unnormalized density itself.

definition.body: Score-based sampling is a human-made generative sampling procedure that draws samples from a target distribution by numerically integrating a stochastic differential equation driven by the score function (gradient of the log-density). The method: (1) start from a simple known distribution (e.g., Gaussian noise), (2) simulate the reverse-time SDE dX/dt = f(X,t) - g(t)^2 * ∇_x log p_t(X) where f is the drift, g is the noise schedule, and ∇_x log p_t is the score function at time t, (3) collect the final state as a sample from the target distribution. The score at each time is approximated by a trained neural network via score matching. Parameters: the noise schedule g(t), the time discretization step, the score network architecture and weights. Persistence: implemented in score-based generative modeling frameworks (SMLD, VESDE), published algorithms (Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015, Song et al. 2021), and used for image, audio, and molecular generation. e.g.: Song et al. 2021 score-based generative modeling via stochastic differential equations; Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015 deep unsupervised learning using nonequilibrium thermodynamics; NCSNv2 score matching with annealed Langevin dynamics for image generation | not: score-function (the derivative object, not the sampling procedure); score-matching (the training method, not the sampling from the trained model) [formal: sectio per gradum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: mel-frequency-cepstral-coefficient
payload.scope: People made the mel-frequency cepstral coefficient to compress spectral shape into a compact, perceptually motivated set of features for speech and audio recognition.

definition.body: The mel-frequency cepstral coefficient is a human-made audio feature that represents the short-time spectral envelope of a signal in a perceptually warped frequency scale followed by a discrete cosine transform. The procedure: (1) compute a short-time magnitude spectrum via STFT, (2) map linear frequency bins to mel-scale triangular filters, (3) compute log filterbank energies, (4) apply a DCT to the log energies to obtain cepstral coefficients. Parameters: number of mel filters, FFT size, window length and hop, number of coefficients retained. Persistence: implemented in speech recognition toolkits (HTK, Kaldi), audio libraries (librosa.feature.mfcc), and taught in digital speech processing courses. e.g.: librosa.feature.mfcc for music and speech analysis; the MFCC front-end in the Kaldi speech recognition toolkit; the MFCC implementation in the HTK speech toolkit | not: mel-spectrogram (log mel filterbank energies before DCT); linear predictive cepstral coefficient (LPCC, derived from linear prediction, not mel filterbank) [formal: coefficient cepstralis mel | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spectral-inversion
payload.scope: People made spectral inversion to transform a spectral envelope into its perceptual complement, enabling voice disguise, creative audio processing, and feature augmentation.

definition.body: The spectral inversion is a human-made audio processing technique that inverts a spectral envelope to generate a perceptually distinct signal while preserving key spectral characteristics. The procedure: (1) compute the log-power spectrum of the input signal, (2) subtract the log-spectrum from a flat or reference spectrum to invert the spectral envelope, (3) optionally add a constant offset to avoid excessive inversion, (4) convert the inverted log-spectrum back to linear magnitude by exponentiation. The inverted spectrum preserves the spectral centroid and relative bandwidth of the original but inverts the formant structure, producing a perceptually transformed signal useful for disguise, creative processing, and as a preprocessing step in voice conversion. Parameters: (1) the input spectrum, (2) the inversion reference (flat spectrum, average spectrum, or target envelope), (3) the inversion depth parameter controlling how completely the envelope is inverted. Persistence mechanism: implemented in audio processing libraries (librosa.invert_spec, OpenSMILE inversion features), used in voice disguise systems, creative audio effects, and as a feature augmentation technique in speech recognition robustness research. e.g.: the spectral inversion feature in OpenSMILE for speaker recognition robustness; librosa.invert_spec function for creative audio transformation; inversion-based voice disguise in privacy-preserving speech systems [formal: invertio spectralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-decomposition
payload.scope: People made cepstral decomposition to separate source and filter components of a signal using quefrency-domain analysis, enabling formant extraction and pitch detection in speech processing.

definition.body: The cepstral decomposition is a human-made signal processing technique that separates a signal into its source (excitation) and filter (resonance) components by analyzing the cepstrum in the quefrency domain. The procedure: (1) compute the power spectrum of the signal via FFT, (2) take the logarithm to compress the dynamic range and linearize convolutive relationships, (3) apply the inverse FFT to obtain the cepstrum, (4) apply a quefrency-domain window (lifter) to isolate either the low-quefrency component (spectral envelope/formant structure) or the high-quefrency component (pitch periodicity/excitation). Parameters: (1) the input signal or its power spectrum, (2) the lifter function and cutoff quefrency separating source from filter components, (3) the window length for the analysis. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech processing toolkits (Praat, Kaldi, librosa), used in speech analysis for formant extraction and pitch detection, and taught in speech science curricula. e.g.: Praat's formant extraction using cepstral smoothing with a 5ms lifter; Kaldi's cepstral mean normalization using low-quefrency coefficients; librosa.feature.mfcc for extracting the spectral envelope via DCT-based cepstral decomposition; speech pitch detection using high-quefrency cepstral peaks in the RAPT algorithm [formal: decompositio cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: dynamic-time-warping
payload.scope: People made dynamic time warping to align sequences of different lengths by finding the optimal non-linear alignment that minimizes the total distance between corresponding points.

definition.body: The dynamic time warping algorithm finds an optimal alignment between two temporal sequences of different lengths by computing a cumulative distance matrix and tracing the minimum-cost path through it. Parameters: the two input sequences of lengths N and M, the local distance function d(i,j) between individual points, the accumulation scheme (typically additive), and boundary conditions (e.g. Sakoe-Chiba band or Itakura parallelogram restricting the warping path). The algorithm fills an N×M cost matrix C(i,j) = d(i,j) + min(C(i-1,j), C(i-1,j-1), C(i,j-1)) and backtracks from C(N,M) to recover the warping path. Persistence: implemented in speech recognition toolkits (Kaldi dtw function), music information retrieval systems (librosa alignment), and taught as a standard sequence alignment method in pattern recognition. e.g.: the DTW alignment in Kaldi for phone-level forced alignment; librosa.dtw for tempo estimation from audio feature sequences; the DTW-based speech recognition implementation in HTK | not: time-warping (signal modification, not sequence alignment); dynamic-programming (general optimization paradigm, not sequence alignment) [formal: iteratio temporalis distortionis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: frame-windowing
payload.scope: People made frame windowing to reduce spectral leakage when analyzing non-stationary signals by applying a tapering function to signal segments.

definition.body: Frame windowing is the application of a weighting function (window function) to a signal segment during short-time analysis. The procedure: extract a frame of N samples from the signal, multiply element-wise by a window function w(n) defined over 0..N-1 (common choices: Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Kaiser), producing a windowed frame that tapers smoothly to near-zero at both edges. The window function controls the trade-off between main-lobe width (frequency resolution) and side-lobe attenuation (spectral leakage). Parameters: frame length N, window type and shape, overlap ratio with neighboring frames, and framing offset. Persistence: implemented as a fixed operation in every spectral analysis pipeline (librosa.util.frame with window parameter, MATLAB spectrogram with window argument, STFT implementations across all DSP libraries). e.g.: applying a Hann window before FFT in librosa.stft; the Hamming window used in MATLAB speechrecognition toolbox frame analysis; Kaiser window applied in GNU Radio spectral estimation blocks | not: frame-blocking (segmenting the signal into frames, not the tapering operation); overlap-add (a reconstruction method, not a windowing operation) [formal: fenestratio per functionem ponderis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: dct-type-ii
payload.scope: People made the type-II discrete cosine transform as the primary variant for lossy data compression because it provides excellent energy compaction for correlated data.

definition.body: The type-II discrete cosine transform (DCT-II) is the most widely used variant of the discrete cosine transform, computing a real-valued frequency-domain representation from real-valued input samples. For an input sequence x(n) of length N, the DCT-II computes X(k) = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n) * cos(pi * (2n+1) * k / (2N)) for k = 0..N-1. Its key property is energy compaction: for highly correlated signals such as audio or image data, most of the signal energy concentrates into a small number of low-frequency DCT coefficients. The DCT-II and its inverse (DCT-III) form an orthogonal transform pair when scaled by sqrt(2/N) for k=0 and sqrt(1/N) for k>0. Persistence: defined as the standard transform in JPEG, MPEG, and MP3 compression standards; implemented in every major numerical library (numpy.fft.dct type=2, scipy.fft.dct, MATLAB dct function with type=2 option). e.g.: the DCT-II used in JPEG image compression for 8x8 block transforms; the MDCT-based audio coding in Opus codec using DCT principles; the DCT-II computation in the MP3 encoder for frequency-domain analysis | not: discrete cosine transform (the general family of four DCT variants, not specifically type-II); discrete sine transform (DST, uses sine basis functions instead of cosine) [formal: transformatio cosinus discretus II | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: delta-features
payload.scope: People made delta features to capture the temporal dynamics and rate of change of spectral features in speech processing.

definition.body: Delta features are the first temporal derivatives of a sequence of base acoustic features (such as MFCCs), computed as a weighted least-squares fit of a straight line over a sliding window of neighboring frames. For a feature sequence f(t), the delta at frame t is computed by fitting d(t) = argmin_d sum_{k=-K}^{K} w(k) * (f(t+k) - (a*t + b))^2, where w(k) is a weighting function (typically symmetric, e.g. [-1, 0, 1] for simple first differences, or optimal weights [-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3] normalized). The window half-width K determines how many neighboring frames are used (commonly K=2). Delta features approximate the velocity of the spectral envelope, capturing phoneme transitions. Persistence: implemented as a standard feature extraction step in all speech recognition toolkits (Kaldi compute-vad-and-extract-features, HTK VFeat delta computation, librosa.feature.delta for mel-spectrograms). e.g.: delta MFCCs computed by Kaldi's compute-vad-and-extract-features for triphone recognition; HTK delta feature extraction in HCopy tool; librosa.feature.delta applied to mel spectrograms for music genre classification | not: delta-cepstral-coefficients (raw cepstral first differences, not velocity from base features); cepstral-smoothing (cepstral-domain smoothing, not temporal differencing) [formal: deltae proprietatum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: quantization-noise-shaping
payload.scope: People made quantization noise shaping to push quantization error away from perceptually sensitive frequency bands in audio and speech coding.

definition.body: Quantization noise shaping is a technique that redistributes the spectral distribution of quantization error by applying a feedback filter that pushes quantization noise into frequency bands where it is less perceptually objectionable. The procedure: replace the quantized output q[n] with e[n] = q[n] - x[n] + a*(e[n-1]) for a first-order predictor a, creating a high-pass noise transfer function H(z) = 1/(1-az^{-1}) for the error e[n]. The parameter a controls the noise spectrum: positive a pushes noise to higher frequencies (common in delta modulation), negative a pushes noise to lower frequencies. The trade-off is that while perceptual quality improves in the passband, noise may increase in the stopband. Persistence: implemented in delta-sigma ADCs, 1-bit DACs, and speech coding (Adaptive Differential Pulse Code Modulation with noise shaping in telecommunications standards, ITU-T G.712 testing). e.g.: first-order noise shaping in delta-sigma analog-to-digital converters for audio applications; noise-shaped quantization in the ADPCM codec within the TIA/EIA-102 standard; 16-bit audio dithering with first-order noise shaping in the SoX audio processing library | not: dithering (adding random noise before quantization to decorrelate error, without spectral shaping); noise-figure (a measure of degradation in signal-to-noise ratio, not a noise redistribution technique) [formal: configuratio erroris quantizationis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: rasta-filter
payload.scope: People made RASTA filtering to remove slow channel-induced spectral variations and track dynamic changes in speech spectral envelopes.

definition.body: RASTA (Relative SpecTral Alteration) filtering applies band-pass filtering to the logarithmic power spectrum of each frequency channel to retain only temporal variations within a specified band (typically 3-35 Hz), removing slow drifts caused by channel effects while preserving speech-relevant dynamics. The procedure: compute the log power spectrum for each frame, then apply a 1D band-pass filter independently along the time axis for each frequency channel. The filter is a cascade of a high-pass and a low-pass filter, each with a pole near 1.0 and a corresponding zero at the origin (high-pass: H_hp(z) = (1-az^{-1})/(1-pz^{-1}), low-pass: H_lp(z) = (1-z^{-1})/(1-pz^{-1}) where p controls the cutoff). The passband isolates the rate of change corresponding to phoneme transitions (3-35 Hz) while attenuating slow channel variations below 3 Hz and rapid noise fluctuations above 35 Hz. Persistence: implemented in the RTTM toolkit, integrated into several robust speech recognition front-ends, and taught as a standard channel-robustness technique in speech processing courses (Hindriks, 1992). e.g.: RASTA filtering in the RTTM toolkit for telephone channel compensation; the RASTA step in the NIST SRE 2000 speaker recognition evaluation front-end; RASTA-based feature extraction in the Kaldi toolkit's rasta-compute-features utility | not: cepstral-mean-normalization (a per-utterance static subtraction that does not band-pass filter the temporal dimension); frame-windowing (a spectral analysis step, not a temporal band-pass filter on log spectra) [formal: filtrum RASTA | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]
